chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
title: Benny Goodman and Glenn Miller on 'the blues'
summary: In Pollack's band Goodman and Miller laughed at Freeman's remark about the blues, later apologizing.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Well, there is no doubt about it. You see, Benny Goodman started a long time before I did and of course, Benny Goodman compared to me, I mean, Benny Goodman was a true genius, at the age of 12 he was a superb clarinet, and I remember -- he was not as involved in jazz as I was, and I remember one time playing with the Pollack band in New York, and we were all sitting around, Glenn Miller, Benny Goodman, Ben Pollack -- But Ben Pollack knew, and I happened to say -- we were talking about a player and I said, 'Well, I don't think he understands how to play the blues,' and they all broke up laughing, because Benny Goodman and Glenn Miller didn't understand what I meant by the blues. They thought that the blues was Ted Lewis and they thought that was a corny remark that I made and years later they were both to come back and apologize to me. They said, 'We didn't know what you were talking about when you said blues.' Glenn Miller specifically; he said, 'Yes?' And I was only quoting Jack Teagarden who called and said, 'let's play the blues,' man, and we knew that the blues but

was something. But Benny Goodman and Glenn Miller didn't. This is 1928 I am talking about. They were putting me on because I mentioned the blues, because they were identifying with something Ted Lewis did, Blues My Naughty Sweetie Gives Me.
The white man's blues, you see, and anyway I don't know what brought that to my mind. Tributaries of thinking.
